title: What Redis is and how it executes commands
goal: By the end you can explain how one Redis thread runs every command in turn, predict when one slow command stalls every other client, and connect to Redis from Java and Kotlin.

warmup.q: One connection runs a Lua script that spins for 1.5 seconds. 300 ms after it starts, another service sends `GET payment:42` on a different connection. Redis 8.10 runs with its default settings. What happens to the GET?
options: It returns at once: it is a different connection, and Redis 8 has I/O threads
It waits about 1.2 seconds, until the script ends, and then returns the value
It fails at once with a BUSY error
It returns at once with the value from before the script started, like a snapshot read
warmup.why: One thread executes every command, so the GET sits unread until the script returns. I/O threads are off by default (`io-threads 1`), and even when they are on they only read, parse and write; they never run commands. BUSY errors start only after a script has run for 5 seconds (`busy-reply-threshold`). And Redis has no snapshot reads: there is never a second command running to read from.

sections.h: Redis is a shared, in-memory map that every service can reach
sections.body:
Start with a problem you already have. Twenty pods of a payment service handle card authorizations. A client retries a payment with the same idempotency key, and the retry lands on a different pod. That pod has to answer "have I seen key `idem:7f3a` before?" A `HashMap` inside each pod can't answer it, because pod 3's memory is invisible to pod 11. The Oracle database can, but every lookup is then a SQL query on a database that has more important work to do.

What you want is one map that all twenty pods share, kept in memory and reachable over the network. The simplest version is a small server process that holds a `HashMap<String, byte[]>` and understands two commands arriving on a TCP connection (a two-way stream of bytes between two programs): `SET key value` and `GET key`.

Push on that design and it breaks. Count authorizations per card: each pod does `GET`, adds one in its own memory, then `SET`. Two pods can both read 41 and both write 42; the worked example below loses four increments in five exactly this way. Store a payment record and you want to change one field without rewriting the whole value. Rank merchants and you want the server to keep them sorted for you. The fix is the same each time: the server should understand the shape of the value and do the operation itself.

That is Redis: a server that keeps data structures in RAM and changes them with commands. A **key** is a name such as `payment:42`. Its value has a type: a string, a hash (a small map of fields), a list, a set, a sorted set, and a few more that lessons 2 and 3 cover. Each type has its own commands. `INCR auths:card:7` adds one on the server. `HINCRBY payment:43 amount 50` changes one field of a hash. A command that doesn't fit the type fails with `WRONGTYPE`.

Memory makes Redis fast, and the network decides how fast. On my laptop a `GET` from the JVM to the Redis container took about 214 microseconds end to end. Redis spent about half a microsecond of that running the command; the rest was the trip through sockets and Docker's virtual network. Keep that ratio in mind for the whole track: round trips cost far more than commands, until one command doesn't. Redis can also save the data to disk so it survives a restart (lesson 10), but reads never come from that copy.

The current release is Redis Open Source 8.10.3, and the labs pin the Docker image `redis:8.10.3`. Its license changed twice: BSD up to 7.2, RSALv2 or SSPLv1 for 7.4 to 7.8, and from 8.0 also AGPLv3. After the 2024 change, AWS and Google backed a BSD-licensed fork run by the Linux Foundation, Valkey, now at 9.1.3. Lessons 1 and 2 work on both, and this track names the version whenever a command needs Redis 8.

try.title: Start Redis and poke it
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the server: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d`.
Open a prompt with `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli` and type the commands below, one at a time.
Before the last three, predict: what does `TYPE` say, and what happens when you `GET` a hash?
Leave the server running for the rest of the lesson. When you are done for the day, stop it and delete its data with `docker compose -f env/redis.yml down -v`.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.src:
PING
SET payment:42 approved
GET payment:42
INCR auths:today
INCR auths:today
HSET payment:43 status approved amount 1250 currency EUR
HINCRBY payment:43 amount 50
TYPE payment:43
GET payment:43
INFO server

try.expect: `PING` answers `PONG` and `GET payment:42` prints `"approved"`. The two `INCR`s print `(integer) 1` and `(integer) 2`: the key didn't exist, so Redis started from 0. `HSET` prints `(integer) 3` (three new fields) and `HINCRBY` prints `(integer) 1300`, computed on the server. `TYPE payment:43` says `hash`, and `GET payment:43` fails with `(error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`. In the `INFO server` output, find `redis_version:8.10.3` and `multiplexing_api:epoll`: the server asks the Linux kernel's epoll which sockets have data. That is the loop in the next section.

sections.h: One thread runs every command, one after another
sections.body:
Now the server has thousands of clients, each on its own TCP connection, all sending commands at once. How should one server process serve them?

The obvious design is one thread per connection, the way a classic Java servlet container works. Each thread reads its client's command, runs it and writes the reply. It breaks in two places. Ten thousand connections need ten thousand threads, each with its own stack, and the operating system spends its time switching between them. Worse, two threads can now touch the same key at the same moment. `INCR auths:card:7` from two threads is the `count++` race again (both read 41, both write 42, one update is lost), this time inside the server, so every key needs a lock and every command pays for locking, even when nobody else is near its key.

Redis goes the other way: one thread runs every command. A single thread must never sit waiting on one quiet socket, so it asks the kernel instead, through a system call (a request a program makes to the operating system). On Linux that call is `epoll_wait`: "here are 10,000 sockets; tell me which ones have bytes ready, and let me sleep until at least one does." Then the thread serves only those. This loop is the **event loop**, and it repeats four steps:

1. Ask the kernel which client sockets have bytes waiting. If none do, sleep until one does.
2. For each ready client, read the bytes and cut them into complete commands.
3. Run each command against memory, to the end, and put the reply in that client's output buffer.
4. Before sleeping again, write the queued replies back to the sockets.

Step 3 is the base model for this whole track. Commands from different clients never overlap. While `INCR auths:card:7` runs, nothing else can read or write anything. So every single command is atomic: it happens as one step, and no client ever sees it half done. Fifty pods calling `INCR` on one key never lose an update, and Redis needs no locks to promise that. Nobody else is running.

The price is the same fact seen from the other side. A command that takes 1.5 seconds holds the only thread for 1.5 seconds, and every other client waits, whatever key it wants. On the lab server a `GET` costs about half a microsecond of that thread's time, so one 1.5-second command costs as much as three million `GET`s. The usual culprits are commands whose cost grows with the size of a key: `KEYS *` over the whole keyspace, `HGETALL` or `SMEMBERS` on a key with a million entries, `DEL` of a huge key, and long Lua scripts. A Lua script is a small program that Redis runs as one command (lesson 6); here it is just the easiest way to keep Redis busy.

Step through the loop below with three clients. The last two frames show one slow script freezing the others.

try.title: Freeze the server with one script
steps: Open two terminals in the `labs` folder. In terminal 2, type this but don't press Enter yet: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli GET payment:42`.
In terminal 1, run the command below. Its Lua script spins on the server's CPU for 3,000 ms. Switch to terminal 2 at once and press Enter. Predict: when does `"approved"` appear?
Run the script again with `7000` in place of `3000`, then the GET. Wait. When the GET gives up, stop the script from terminal 2: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli SCRIPT KILL`.

code.title: terminal 1
code.src: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli EVAL "local stop = os.clock() + ARGV[1] / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1" 0 3000

try.expect: The GET hangs, and prints `"approved"` a moment after terminal 1 prints `(integer) 1`. A different connection and an unrelated key made no difference. With 7000 ms the GET doesn't wait to the end: at the 5-second mark it fails with `(error) BUSY Redis is busy running a script. You can only call SCRIPT KILL or SHUTDOWN NOSAVE.` Five seconds is the default `busy-reply-threshold`. From then on Redis pauses the script now and then to answer other clients, but only with that error, so that you can send `SCRIPT KILL`. It prints `OK`, and terminal 1 gets `(error) ERR Script killed by user with SCRIPT KILL...`. The kill works only because the script has not written anything. A script that has written can only be stopped with `SHUTDOWN NOSAVE`.

sections.h: Redis has several threads, and still only one runs commands
sections.body:
If one thread runs everything, two questions follow. Some jobs are slow by nature: writing a snapshot of 2 GB of data to disk, or freeing the memory of a key with ten million members. Who does those without freezing the loop? And the machine has 8 or 16 cores. Is one thread really all Redis uses?

For the slow jobs, Redis hands the work to helpers that never run commands. The `redis.conf` file that ships with 8.10 calls Redis "mostly single threaded":

- Background threads, named `bio_*` for background I/O, close files, push Redis's on-disk log of writes from memory onto the disk with `fsync`, and free memory for `UNLINK` and `FLUSHALL ASYNC`. Deleting a huge key with `UNLINK` returns at once. Plain `DEL` frees the memory on the main thread while everyone waits.
- To save a snapshot of the whole dataset, Redis starts a copy of itself with `fork`, and that child process writes the file while the parent keeps serving clients (lesson 10).

For the cores, look at where the time goes for a small command. Running a `GET` takes half a microsecond. Reading the request from the socket, parsing it and writing the reply are system calls into the kernel plus copying, and together they often cost more than the command. So Redis 6 added **I/O threads**: helpers that do steps 2 and 4 of the loop (read, parse, write) for many connections in parallel, while the main thread still runs every command in step 3. Redis 8.0 shipped a new implementation of them.

I/O threads are off by default: `io-threads 1` means the main thread does all the I/O itself. The config file says to enable them only on machines with 4 or more cores, and to leave one core spare: 3 I/O threads on 4 cores, 7 on 8. Redis measured up to 112% more throughput for 8.0 with 8 I/O threads on a multi-core Intel server. That is a vendor benchmark, and the gain depends on the command mix.

What I/O threads can't do is run two commands at once or make one command faster. They help a server that spends its time moving bytes for many small commands over thousands of connections. They do nothing for a slow `HGETALL`. When someone says "just add threads", first ask which step of the loop is busy.

try.title: Count the server's threads
steps: List the threads of the running server with the command below. Linux keeps one folder per thread under `/proc/1/task`, and `comm` holds the thread's name.

Start a throwaway server with four I/O threads: `docker run --rm -d --name sfz-io4 -m 128m redis:8.10.3 redis-server --io-threads 4`. List its threads with the same loop, using `docker exec sfz-io4` in place of `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis`.
Try to change it at run time: `docker exec sfz-io4 redis-cli CONFIG SET io-threads 2`. Then remove it: `docker rm -f sfz-io4`.

code.title: terminal
code.src: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis sh -c 'for t in /proc/1/task/*; do cat $t/comm; done'

try.expect: The default server lists six threads: `redis-server` (the main thread, the only one that runs commands), `bio_close_file`, `bio_aof`, `bio_lazy_free`, and two `jemalloc_bg_thd` that belong to the memory allocator. The `--io-threads 4` server adds `io_thd_1`, `io_thd_2` and `io_thd_3`; the main thread counts as I/O thread 0. `CONFIG SET io-threads 2` fails with `can't set immutable config`: you pick the I/O thread count when the server starts.

sections.h: Commands travel as RESP, and clients now speak RESP3
sections.body:
A TCP connection carries a stream of bytes with no boundaries in it. If a client sends two commands quickly, the server may receive both in one read, or half of one. So the server needs a rule for where one command ends and the next begins.

The simplest rule is text lines: `SET payment:42 approved`, then a newline. Redis still accepts that from someone typing into a raw connection. It breaks as soon as a value contains a space or a newline, and values do: a JSON document, a serialized Java object, any bytes at all. Quoting rules would force the server to inspect every byte of every value.

The fix is to send each length first. That is **RESP**, the Redis serialization protocol. A command is an array of strings, each with its length in bytes in front:

```text
*2\r\n$3\r\nGET\r\n$10\r\npayment:42\r\n
```

Read it as: an array (`*`) of 2 elements, a 3-byte string (`$3`) `GET`, a 10-byte string `payment:42`. `\r\n` is a carriage return and a line feed, the line ending. Because the server knows each length up front, it reads exactly that many bytes and never looks inside them. The first byte of a reply says what kind of reply it is: `+OK` is a simple string, `:42` an integer, `$8` an 8-byte string, `$-1` no value, `-ERR` an error.

That version is RESP2, the standard since Redis 2.0. It has one gap: structured replies come back as flat arrays. `HGETALL` returns `status`, `approved`, `amount`, `1250`, and the client has to know to pair them up. RESP3, available since Redis 6.0, adds real maps (`%`), sets (`~`), doubles, booleans, a null (`_`), and push messages that the server sends without being asked, which client-side caching relies on. Every connection starts in RESP2 and switches when the client sends `HELLO 3`.

Both Java clients in this track send `HELLO 3` when they connect. Jedis 8 made that its default, and falls back to RESP2 if the server refuses. You will rarely look at RESP. You need it when a proxy mangles traffic, when a reply type surprises your code, or when you read a packet capture.

sections.h: This track uses Jedis, and Lettuce where Kotlin needs it
sections.body:
Nobody should format RESP by hand, so you use a client library. The interesting choice inside a client is how the threads of your service share TCP connections.

The first design is a pool. The client keeps several open connections. A call borrows one, sends one command, waits for the reply and gives the connection back. While one thread waits, others use other connections. Every call blocks its thread for one round trip, and threads queue when all connections are busy: Jedis's pool holds at most 8 connections unless you configure more, so 200 request threads on 8 connections take turns. This is Jedis.

The second design is multiplexing: one connection shared by every thread. Calls write their commands onto the same socket back to back, without waiting for each other. Redis answers the commands on a connection in the order they arrived, so the client keeps a queue of callers and hands each reply to the next caller in line. One connection carries thousands of calls in flight. The cost is that your code gets a future, a callback or a suspended coroutine instead of a plain value. This is Lettuce.

Jedis 8.0.2 gives you one `RedisClient`, built with `RedisClient.builder()`, with the pool behind it. Lettuce 7.9.0, built on Netty, has a sync API, an async API that returns `RedisFuture` (a `CompletionStage`), a reactive API on Project Reactor, and a Kotlin coroutines API. The coroutines API is a layer over the reactive one, so it needs both `kotlinx-coroutines-core` and `kotlinx-coroutines-reactive` on the classpath, and an opt-in annotation, `@ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi`.

**This track teaches with Jedis.** One call is one command and one reply, so your code maps line for line onto what you type in `redis-cli`, and the lessons stay about Redis instead of about futures. Lettuce shows up where it changes the picture: Kotlin coroutines, and many calls sharing one connection. If your Quarkus services use the Quarkus Redis extension, that one is built on the Vert.x Redis client and works like Lettuce: non-blocking, few connections.

One trap: both libraries name their entry class `RedisClient`. In a file that uses both, write one of them with its full package name.

```java
RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build();
redis.set("payment:42", "approved");
String status = redis.get("payment:42");          // blocks until the reply arrives
```

```kotlin
val redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()
redis.set("payment:42", "approved")
val status: String? = redis.get("payment:42")     // GET of a missing key returns null
```

refs.title: Jedis v7 to v8 migration guide

analogy: A Redis server is a bank branch with one very fast teller and many doors. Customers queue at their own door. The teller takes the request at the front of each door in turn, finishes it completely, puts the receipt in that door's tray and moves on. No two requests are ever half-done at the same time, so the ledger stays consistent without anyone locking anything. But a customer who asks the teller to count a sack of coins holds up every door. I/O threads are assistants who carry requests to the counter and receipts back, but only the teller touches the ledger. The analogy breaks on speed: a real teller needs a minute per customer, while Redis needs about half a microsecond, so queues that would be hopeless in a bank stay invisible in Redis until one slow request arrives.
in_your_world: Your payment service probably already uses Redis for idempotency keys, rate limits or a cache of card-issuer responses. All of them share one execution thread with every other service on that Redis. When the fraud team's nightly job runs `KEYS fraud:*` on the shared instance, your authorization path's `GET idem:...` calls wait behind it, and your p99 jumps from 1 ms to however long that command takes. Nothing in your service changed, and the Redis host's CPU graph looks calm: one core is busy and the rest are idle. Two habits follow. Treat every command on a big key as a cost that every client pays. And when Redis latency spikes for all keys at once, look for one slow command first (`SLOWLOG GET`), before you look at the network or ask for more threads.
mistake: The most common mistake is reading "single-threaded" as "slow" or "can't use more cores", and then fixing the wrong thing. Teams turn on `io-threads` or buy a bigger instance when the real problem is one O(N) command, one whose cost grows with the size of a key: a `KEYS *`, an `HGETALL` on a hash that grew to a million fields, a `DEL` of a huge set, a Lua script that loops over thousands of keys. More cores can't help, because only one thread executes commands. Find the command instead: `SLOWLOG GET` lists every command that took longer than 10 ms (the default `slowlog-log-slower-than` is 10000 microseconds). Then replace it with an incremental one: `SCAN` for `KEYS`, `HSCAN` for `HGETALL`, `UNLINK` for `DEL`, and several smaller keys for one giant key.

kotlin.title: PaymentStatus.kt

Kotlin gets it with `async` and `await`, and the code reads top to bottom. The coroutines API is a layer over Lettuce's reactive API, which is why it needs `kotlinx-coroutines-reactive` on the classpath and an opt-in annotation. Jedis code looks the same in both languages: it blocks, so there is nothing to translate.

worked.title: Count authorizations from eight threads without losing any

steps.say: A settlement job counts today's authorizations in Redis. Eight worker threads share one Jedis `RedisClient`, and each one reads the counter, adds 1 and writes it back. Predict what it prints after 8,000 calls.

Three runs against the lab server printed 1,611, then 1,654, then 1,628. About four in five increments vanished. Each command was atomic, but the pair was not. Between one thread's `GET` and its `SET`, the event loop ran other threads' commands, so several threads read the same old value and wrote the same new one. It is `count++` again, with a network round trip widening the gap.

Let the server do the read, the add and the write as one command. `INCR` runs to completion inside the loop, so nothing can come between its read and its write. The same job now prints 8000 on every run.

With Lettuce, Kotlin can send all 8,000 `INCR`s from coroutines over a single connection, with no thread pool at all. Each `incr` suspends until its reply arrives, and the commands queue up on the one socket. On the lab server this took about 230 ms (it depends on your machine and Docker) and printed 8000. The Java twin uses the async API and waits with `CompletableFuture.allOf`.

lab.title: Model the event loop, then catch the real one blocking
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All eight fail: five in `EventLoopTest`, a model that needs no Docker, and three in `SlowScriptProbeTest`, which run against a real Redis 8.10 container that Testcontainers starts for you.
Write `EventLoop.runUntilIdle()` in `EventLoop.kt`. The KDoc lists the four steps. Take the snapshot of arrived commands once per pass, before you run any of them.

Run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.redis.l01.EventLoopTest'` until its five tests pass. Read the test `a command that arrives during a pass waits for the next pass`: the real loop behaves the same way.

Write `timeGet` and `timeGetDuringScript` in `SlowScriptProbe.java`. Start the script on the `scripts` client in a background thread, sleep `HEAD_START_MS`, time the GET on the `app` client, then wait for the script.
Run all eight tests. The Docker tests take a few seconds, because they block the server on purpose.
hints: `pending.filter { it.arrivedAt <= clock }` gives you the snapshot. Loop over `clients`, and inside that over the snapshot entries of that client, so each client's commands keep their order.
If nothing has arrived, set `clock = pending.minOf { it.arrivedAt }` and go round again. Without that, an idle loop spins forever and the test times out.

`CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> scripts.eval(BUSY_SCRIPT, 0, String.valueOf(scriptMillis)))` runs the script in the background. Call `join()` on it before you return, so a script error fails the call.

drill.title: Write the slow-script probe from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write `timeGetDuringScript(scripts, app, key, millis)`: start a busy Lua script on one client in the background, wait 200 ms, time a `GET` on the other client, wait for the script, and return the GET's milliseconds. Write the Lua too. Then compare with the answer. Did you remember why the script needs its own thread?

alt.src:
const val BUSY = "local stop = os.clock() + tonumber(ARGV[1]) / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1"

fun timeGetDuringScript(scripts: RedisClient, app: RedisClient, key: String, millis: Long): Long {
    val script = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { scripts.eval(BUSY, 0, millis.toString()) }   // eval blocks a pool thread
    Thread.sleep(200)                       // head start: the script is running
    val t0 = System.nanoTime()
    app.get(key)                            // waits for the script to end
    val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000
    script.join()
    return ms
}

recap: Redis keeps typed data structures in memory, and commands change them on the server, so you rarely read, modify and write back.
One thread runs every command, one after another, each to completion. That makes every single command atomic without any locks.
The same fact lets one slow command (`KEYS *`, `HGETALL` on a huge hash, a long Lua script) stall every client, whatever key it wants.
Background threads, a forked child and optional I/O threads (`io-threads`, off by default) do side work. None of them executes commands.
Clients speak RESP. Jedis 8 and Lettuce 7.9 both switch their connections to RESP3 with `HELLO 3`.
This track teaches with Jedis's blocking `RedisClient`, and uses Lettuce for Kotlin coroutines and many async calls over one connection.

quiz.q: Fifty pods each call `INCR auths:today` 1,000 times on the same key, all at the same moment. No call times out or retries. What does the key hold at the end?
options: Exactly 50,000
Less than 50,000, because some increments overlap
Exactly 50,000 only if `io-threads` is off
A different number on every run
quiz.why: Each `INCR` reads, adds and writes inside one command, and the loop never runs two commands at once. I/O threads only move bytes; they never execute commands, so turning them on changes nothing here. Overlapping increments are a client-side bug (GET then SET), not something one `INCR` can suffer.

quiz.q: Two pods debit the same balance at once with `String v = redis.get("balance:7"); redis.set("balance:7", String.valueOf(Long.parseLong(v) - 100));`. Each command is atomic. Is the debit safe?
options: Yes, because each command is atomic
No: both pods can read the same balance before either writes, so one debit is lost
Yes, as long as both pods share one Jedis `RedisClient`
No, because the `GET` and the `SET` may go over two different pooled connections
quiz.why: Atomic commands don't make a sequence of commands atomic. The loop can run the other pod's `GET` between your `GET` and your `SET`. Use one command that does the whole job (`DECRBY balance:7 100`), or a script or transaction (lesson 6). Which connection carries each command doesn't matter either: the gap is between two commands on the server, and sharing one client object or one connection doesn't close it.

quiz.q: Your Redis p99 jumps from 1 ms to 900 ms for a few seconds every hour, for every key. During the spike one CPU core is at 100% and the others are idle. What do you check first?
options: Turn on `io-threads 4` to use the idle cores
Raise the Jedis pool size so more requests are in flight
Look in `SLOWLOG GET` for one slow command that runs at that time
Switch the clients to RESP3 so replies parse faster
quiz.why: Every key slowing down together, with one core pegged, is the signature of one long command holding the only execution thread. `SLOWLOG` names it. I/O threads and more connections can't help, because the bottleneck is command execution, and that stays on one thread.

quiz.q: Which of these does Redis 8.10 do off the main thread with its default settings?
options: Executing `GET` and `SET`
Running Lua scripts
Reading and parsing commands from client sockets
Freeing the memory of a big key deleted with `UNLINK`
quiz.why: `UNLINK` hands the memory to the `bio_lazy_free` background thread. Commands and scripts always run on the main thread. Reading and parsing move to I/O threads only when you start the server with `io-threads` above 1, and the default is 1.

quiz.q: A Lua script has been spinning for 6 seconds on a Redis with default settings. A client sends `GET payment:42`. What does that client get?
options: A BUSY error at once, because the script is past the 5-second `busy-reply-threshold`
The value, as soon as the script finishes
The value at once, because reads skip the script queue
A connection reset
quiz.why: After 5 seconds Redis starts answering other clients between script steps, but only with BUSY errors, so that someone can send `SCRIPT KILL` (or `SHUTDOWN NOSAVE` if the script has written). Before the 5-second mark the same GET would simply wait.

flashcards.front: How many threads execute commands in Redis 8?
flashcards.back: One, the main thread. Background threads, a forked child and optional I/O threads do side work, never command execution.

flashcards.front: Why can fifty clients call `INCR` on one key without losing an update?
flashcards.back: The event loop runs each command to completion before it starts the next, so no other command can run between INCR's read and its write.
Three extra threads, plus the main one, read sockets, parse commands and write replies. Commands still run one at a time on the main thread. You can set it only at start-up.

flashcards.front: What happens to other clients while a Lua script runs?
flashcards.back: They wait. After `busy-reply-threshold` (5 s by default) they get BUSY errors until the script ends or someone runs `SCRIPT KILL`.

flashcards.front: How does a client switch its connection to RESP3?
flashcards.back: It sends `HELLO 3`. Jedis 8 and Lettuce 7.9 both do this when they connect.

flashcards.front: What does Lettuce's Kotlin coroutines API need?
flashcards.back: `kotlinx-coroutines-core` and `kotlinx-coroutines-reactive` on the classpath, and an `@OptIn(ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi::class)`.

terms.plain: A loop that waits for sockets with data, runs what arrived, and writes the replies. Redis's main thread is one.
Happens as one step. Other clients see it either not started or finished, never halfway.
The Linux call a server uses to ask which of thousands of sockets have data, without one thread per socket.
The Redis serialization protocol: length-prefixed strings, integers, arrays and errors. RESP3 adds maps, sets, a null and push messages.
Optional threads (`io-threads`) that read, parse and write for the main thread. They never run commands.
A set of open connections that calls borrow one at a time and give back. Jedis keeps at most 8 by default.
Many callers sharing one connection: commands go out back to back, and replies are matched to callers in order.
A BSD-licensed fork of Redis, run by the Linux Foundation.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Redis is single-threaded, so it can't keep up with us. Let's turn on I/O threads so it runs our commands in parallel." Explain what is right and what is wrong in that, in your own words.
explain_back.answer: Redis does execute commands on one thread, one at a time, each to completion. That is why each command is atomic, and why one slow command makes everyone wait. But one thread is rarely the limit for small commands: a GET costs about half a microsecond. I/O threads don't run commands in parallel. They take over reading sockets, parsing commands and writing replies, which helps when the server spends its time on network bytes for many connections. If our problem is latency spikes, the likely cause is one slow O(N) command, and I/O threads won't touch it. I'd check `SLOWLOG GET` first and replace the slow command with an incremental one.

deeper.body:
Why is one thread fast enough? Most commands touch one key and finish in well under a microsecond, the data is already in RAM, and with no second thread there are no locks to take and no cache lines bouncing between cores. For small commands the expensive part is usually the system calls: one `read` and one `write` per command per client. That is the cost pipelining attacks (lesson 6: send many commands, read many replies, pay the syscalls once) and I/O threads spread over cores.

The real loop is a little richer than the lab's model. When a client has sent several commands at once, Redis reads a buffer's worth of bytes and runs every complete command in it before moving to the next client. That is why a pipelined batch from one client runs back to back, and why a client that sends a huge batch can delay the clients after it in the same pass.

One thing surprised me while writing this lesson. The first busy script I tried looped on `redis.call('TIME')` until 2,000 ms had passed. It ran for 5 seconds instead. Inside a script, `TIME` kept returning the moment the script started, and it only moved when the 5-second busy handling kicked in. `os.clock()` measures CPU time, which keeps moving, so the lab uses it. If you ever write a script that waits on server time, it won't work for the same reason, and you shouldn't want a script that waits anyway.

If you want the source, `src/ae.c` in the Redis repository is the event loop library (it wraps epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS), and `src/networking.c` reads queries and writes replies.
